name: The two natures of the Lord (aparā and parā prakṛti)

definitions.definition: BhG 7.4–7: the Lord's lower nature is eightfold — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, I-maker; his higher nature has become the living being and upholds the world. All beings have these two as their source; he is the origin and dissolution of the whole world; nothing is higher than him, and all is strung on him like gems on a thread.

members: parā prakṛti jīvabhūtā (the higher nature, become the living being)

definitions.definition: BhG 7.16–18: four kinds of people of good deeds worship the Lord — the distressed (ārta), the one who wishes to know (jijñāsu), the seeker of gain (arthārthin) and the knower (jñānin). All are noble; the knower, ever yoked and of single devotion, is foremost, mutually dear with the Lord, and held by him to be his very self.

name: The three planes: divine, bodily, sacrificial

definitions.definition: BhG 7.29–8.4 gives a set of six things to be known with the Lord and defines each: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; adhyātma is (its) own being (svabhāva); karma is the emission that brings beings into existence; adhibhūta is the perishable state; adhidaivata is the Person (puruṣa); adhiyajña is the Lord himself here in the body. Those who know him so know him even at the time of departure.

members: adhiyajña = the Lord in the body

definitions.definition: BhG 8.5–7: whoever departs remembering the Lord alone at the time of the end comes to his state; whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes, having always been shaped by it; therefore one should remember him at all times (and, for Arjuna, fight).

relations.note: the yogin's form of the last remembrance (8.10–13)

name: The day and night of Brahmā

definitions.definition: BhG 8.17–19: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand ages and his night likewise; at the coming of day all manifest things come forth from the unmanifest, at the coming of night they dissolve into it; the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly. Even Brahmā's world is a world of return (8.16).

name: The two paths after death: of the gods and of the fathers

names.name: śukla-kṛṣṇe gatī (the bright and dark courses)

definitions.definition: BhG 8.23–27 speaks of two everlasting courses of the departed, the bright and the dark: fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the six months of the northern course lead knowers of Brahman to Brahman and non-return; smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the six months of the southern course lead the yogin to the lunar light and return. The yogin who knows the two is not deluded.

members: śukla gati: agni, jyotis, ahaḥ, śukla pakṣa, uttarāyaṇa → brahman, anāvṛtti
kṛṣṇa gati: dhūma, rātri, kṛṣṇa pakṣa, dakṣiṇāyana → cāndramasaṃ jyotiḥ, āvṛtti

definitions.definition: BhG 8: Brahman is the supreme imperishable (8.3); the imperishable is what knowers of the Veda declare and passionless ascetics enter (8.11); beyond the cosmic unmanifest there is another eternal unmanifest, called the imperishable, the supreme goal from which there is no return, the Lord's supreme abode (8.20–21).

In BhG 7 and 9 the Lord names himself the essence in things — the taste in water, the light of sun and moon, Oṃ in the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, fragrance in earth, radiance in fire, life in beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed, intelligence, brilliance, strength free of passion, desire not opposed to dharma (7.8–11) — and every element of the sacrifice, father, mother, ordainer, grandsire, Oṃ and the Vedas, goal, witness, refuge, friend, origin, dissolution, immortality and death, being and non-being (9.16–19).

BhG 7.14–15, 7.25: the Lord's divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross; those who take refuge in him alone cross it; it carries off the knowledge of evil-doers; veiled by his yoga-māyā he is not manifest to all.

name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: BhG 7 and 9 contrast those who resort to the demonic state or the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras — evil-doers of vain hopes, acts and knowledge who do not take refuge in the Lord and disregard him in human form (7.15; 9.11–12) — with the great-souled who resort to the divine nature (daivī prakṛti) and worship him with undivided mind (9.13).

BhG 9.20–21: knowers of the three Vedas who drink soma and sacrifice pray for the way to heaven, reach the world of the lord of the gods and enjoy divine pleasures; when their merit is spent they return to the mortal world — the 'going and coming' of those who follow the triple dharma with desire.

BhG 7–9: all beings fall into delusion at birth (7.27); after many births the knower takes refuge (7.19); rebirth is the impermanent abode of sorrow, and all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return, but those who reach the Lord are not reborn (8.15–16); the multitude of beings comes to be again and again (8.19); the faithless return to the path of death and saṃsāra (9.3); sacrificers return when merit is spent (9.21).

name: Creation and dissolution of the world

definitions.definition: BhG 7–9: the Lord is the origin and dissolution of the whole world (7.6; 9.18); at the close of a kalpa beings go into his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth again, taking hold of his prakṛti (9.7–8); prakṛti brings forth the moving and unmoving with him as overseer (9.10); manifest things arise from and dissolve into the unmanifest with Brahmā's day and night (8.18–19). These acts do not bind him (9.9).

BhG 7.12–14: states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from the Lord, he not in them but they in him; the world, deluded by these three guṇa-made states, does not know him who is beyond them; his divine māyā is made of the guṇas.

BhG 7.24–25 and 9.11 (without the word avatāra): the deluded disregard the Lord when he has taken on a human body, not knowing his higher state as great Lord of beings; the unintelligent think the unmanifest has come into manifestation; he is veiled by his yoga-māyā.

BhG 8.10–13: at the time of departure the yogin, with unmoving mind, devotion and the power of yoga, makes the breath enter between the brows and reaches the supreme divine Person; restraining all the gates, confining the mind in the heart, placing the breath in the head, established in yogic concentration, uttering Oṃ and remembering the Lord, he goes to the supreme goal.

BhG 7 and 9: taking refuge in the Lord alone crosses his māyā (7.14); the knower takes refuge after many births (7.19); those striving for release from old age and death take refuge in him (7.29); by taking refuge in him even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal (9.32).
BhG 9.9: the acts of sending forth the beings do not bind the Lord, who is seated as one indifferent, unattached to those acts.
BhG 7–9: the Lord is the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8) and the oṃkāra along with the three Vedas (9.17); Oṃ is 'the one-syllabled Brahman', uttered at departure while remembering the Lord (8.13).

name: The Lord's lordly yoga: beings in him, he not in them (yoga aiśvara)

definitions.definition: BhG 9.4–6 with 7.12: all this is pervaded by the Lord in unmanifest form; all beings abide in him, but he is not established in them; and yet beings do not abide in him — 'behold my lordly yoga'; sustaining beings and bringing them into being, his self does not abide in them; as the great wind moving everywhere abides in space, so all beings abide in him. States of the guṇas are from him, he not in them, they in him.

notes: New concept id for the Gītā's own phrase; the text leaves the paradox of 9.4–5 unresolved.

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: BhG 9.1–2: the teaching is 'most secret', the royal secret, declared to one who does not cavil (anasūyu); it is royal knowledge, purifying, directly apprehended, in accord with dharma and easy to practise.
BhG 7.26: the Lord knows all beings past, present and to come, but no one knows him.

name: Kalpa, the day of Brahmā and his lifetime

definitions.definition: BhG 8.17 and 9.7: Brahmā's day and night are each a thousand ages; at the close of a kalpa beings go into the Lord's prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth.

name: Iṣṭāpūrta, merit of sacrifice and gift

definitions.definition: BhG 8.28, 9.20–21: the merit declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts wins heaven, is exhausted, and brings return to the mortal world; the yogin who knows the teaching passes beyond all such merit to the supreme primal place.

BhG 7 and 9 (without the word prasāda): the Lord makes the worshipper's faith unwavering and ordains the fruits obtained (7.21–22); for the undivided devotee he himself carries acquisition and preservation (yoga-kṣema) (9.22); for the constant rememberer he is easy to reach (8.14).
BhG 7.5: the Lord's higher nature 'has become the living being' (jīvabhūtā) and upholds the world.

name: Varṇa — the four classes, as the tradition states it

definitions.definition: BhG 9.32–33: taking refuge in the Lord, even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal — how much more holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers.
